name: Hinduism
era: From the Vedas, about 1500 BCE, to today
line: Do your duty with love, offer the result and see the sacred in everything.

quote.text: Be intent on action, not on the fruits of action.
quote.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.47, trans. Barbara Stoler Miller

quotes.text: Truth is one; the wise call it by many names.
quotes.source: Rig Veda 1.164.46, in its common English rendering

quotes.text: Lead me from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, from death to immortality.
quotes.source: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.3.28, in its common English rendering

quotes.text: Let noble thoughts come to us from every side.
quotes.source: Rig Veda 1.89.1, in its common English rendering

quotes.text: Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer or give away, do it as an offering to me.
quotes.source: Bhagavad Gita 9.27, paraphrased from several translations

words.meaning: Duty, right order, the way to live
words.usage: What holds the world and a life together. It changes with your age, your work and the people who depend on you.
Every act leaves a trace that returns, in this life or another. It means deed before it means fate.

words.meaning: The round of birth and death
words.usage: The wandering of the self from life to life until it is free.
The end of the round. The fourth and last aim of human life.
The innermost self, which the Upanishads say is not born and does not die.
The ground of everything. Not to be confused with Brahma the creator god or the brahmin priest.
The way of the heart: love for a chosen form of God, shown in song, service and worship.
Honouring a deity as an honoured guest, with water, flowers, light, incense and food.
The heart of a temple visit. You look at the deity and the deity looks at you.
Food that has been offered and comes back as a gift. It is shared with everyone present.
A form in which the deity is invited to be present. Better translated as embodiment than as idol.
A house of the deity. Many homes also have a small shrine in a corner or a cupboard.
Said with the palms together. A greeting that honours the person in front of you.
The sound that opens and closes prayers. The Mandukya Upanishad treats it as the whole of reality in one breath.
Words whose power lies in their sound and repetition as well as their meaning.
Often counted on a string of 108 beads called a mala.
Any steady path that joins the self to what is highest. Postures are one small part of it.
Doing no injury in act, word or thought. The root of much Hindu vegetarianism.
Work done for others with no thought of return, as an offering.
The one who removes darkness. A relationship of trust that is entered slowly.
The form of the divine a person feels closest to. Families and regions have theirs too.
Vishnu coming into the world when order fails, as Rama, Krishna and others.
The idea that the world is God’s play, made from joy and for no gain.
The energy that moves everything, worshipped as Durga, Kali, Lakshmi and many others.
The second aim of life. Earning a living honestly is a duty of the householder.
The third aim of life: beauty, affection and delight, enjoyed within dharma.
Student, householder, forest dweller and renouncer: four seasons, each with its own duties.
A place of pilgrimage, often at a river, where this world and the other are close.
A lamp circled before the deity while a hymn is sung. The flame is then offered to each person.
Said three times at the end of a prayer: peace in oneself, in others and in the world.

practices.name: The morning offering
practices.instructions: Wash first. Then stand or sit facing the early light. Put your palms together and take three slow breaths. Offer something simple: a glass of fresh water, a flower or a lit candle on a clean shelf or windowsill. Say in your own words, or in silence, thank you for this day. Leave the offering where you will see it through the day.
practices.why: In a Hindu home the day begins clean and with an offering, however small. The offering turns the first minutes into a moment of thanks rather than hurry.
variations: Offer a glass of water to a plant instead.
Offer the first sip of your tea to the window.
Offer a flower picked on the way home yesterday.

practices.name: Work without the fruit
practices.instructions: Before your main task of the day, name it and name the result you are hoping for: praise, payment, a win. Then set that result down for the length of the task. Decide to do the work as well as it can be done because it is yours to do. When you finish, notice how it feels to have done it without bargaining.
practices.why: The Bhagavad Gita teaches that you have a right to the action but not to its fruits. Working fully while letting go of the result is the heart of karma yoga.
variations: Do it for a task you dislike.
Do it for a task someone else will take credit for.
Write the hoped-for result on paper and put it in a drawer.

practices.name: Look at your palms
practices.instructions: As soon as you wake, before you touch anything, sit up and look at your open palms for a few breaths. An old waking verse says the goddess of wealth lives at the fingertips, the goddess of learning in the middle of the hand and the lord at its base, and that you should look at your hands at dawn. Take it as a reminder that your hands will do the day’s work. Then rub them together and warm your face.
practices.why: The verse karagre vasate lakshmih is taught to children across India as a first thought of the day. It points you to the hands that will give, make and serve.
variations: Say the verse aloud if you know it.
Thank your hands for one thing they did yesterday.
Massage each hand for a minute.

practices.name: A gentle sun greeting
practices.instructions: Face the light. Stand with palms together, raise your arms, bow forward with bent knees, rise halfway with a flat back, and come up again. Do this slowly, six times, in time with your breath: in as you rise, out as you bend. Stay standing if you like. Skip any bend that hurts your back or knees. Surya namaskar means greeting the sun.
practices.why: The sun salutation is a morning habit in much of India, a flowing greeting to the light. A gentle version wakes the body without strain.
variations: Add a full stretch up on tiptoe.
Do it outdoors on the grass.
Count the rounds on your fingers.

practices.name: Water a living thing
practices.instructions: Water a plant, a tree or a pot of herbs with a small jug, slowly, and say one word of thanks as you pour. In many Hindu homes a tulsi plant stands in the courtyard and is watered each morning. If you have no plants, fill a bowl for the birds. Care for one living thing before you care for yourself.
practices.why: Caring for plants and animals before the day starts is an old household custom. The rule of this Onda is to do no harm and to feed someone first.
variations: Fill a bowl for the birds on your sill.
Water a plant for a neighbour.
Plant a seed.

practices.name: Draw a threshold pattern
practices.instructions: With chalk, flour or rice powder, draw a pattern on the step or the floor at your door: a ring of dots joined by loops, or a simple flower with eight petals. In south India this is a kolam, redrawn each dawn and walked over by the end of the day. Make it quickly, and do not mind if it is not even.
practices.why: The kolam and rangoli are drawn fresh every morning and are meant to be wiped away. They welcome guests and teach a gentle lesson about making something beautiful that does not last.
variations: Use coloured chalk on a pavement.
Draw with rice flour so that birds can eat it.
Make a pattern with flower petals instead.

practices.name: Japa: 108 breaths of a name
practices.instructions: Sit comfortably with your back straight. Choose one short phrase and keep it for the whole Onda. Om is the simplest. Om shanti, peace, is another. Repeat it quietly once for each out-breath and count on your fingers or on a string of beads. Do not worry about reaching 108. When the mind wanders, come back to the phrase and begin again.
practices.why: Japa, the repetition of a name or sound, is a basic Hindu practice, with beads called a mala. A steady word gives the mind something to rest on.
variations: Use a knotted string as a mala.
Whisper the phrase with each step of a short walk.
Repeat it silently on the bus.

practices.name: Seva: one act of service
practices.instructions: Do one useful thing for someone else and tell no one. Cook for a neighbour, feed birds, carry something, clean a shared space, give time to someone lonely. Choose the act in the morning so that it happens. While you do it, let go of the thought of thanks. When it is done, put your palms together for a moment and go on with the day.
practices.why: Seva, selfless service, is a part of Hindu life from the household to the temple kitchen. The act is the gift, and anonymity keeps it clean.
variations: Serve at a community kitchen.
Do a chore at home that nobody notices.
Give an hour to a person who is alone.

practices.name: Feed a creature
practices.instructions: Put out food for an animal today: seeds for birds, water for a stray, a bowl of grain or a leaf for a creature that lives near you. Feeding a cow, a crow or an ant is counted as a good deed in Hindu households. Watch quietly for a few minutes. Do no harm, and wash the bowl afterwards.
practices.why: Ahimsa, non-harm, extends to all living things. Feeding the creatures around the house is a daily kindness in many Hindu homes.
variations: Scatter a pinch of sugar or flour near an ant trail.
Put out a shallow dish of water in the heat.
Sit and count the birds that come.

practices.name: See the divine in everyone
practices.instructions: For the next hour, greet every person you meet with namaste, palms together, and a thought: the light in me honours the light in you. Say it silently or aloud. Do it with the cashier, the neighbour and the person you do not like. Notice how it changes your face and your voice. Namaste means I bow to you.
practices.why: Namaste is an everyday greeting, and also a small teaching: the same spirit is in all beings. Practising it makes you slower to judge and quicker to smile.
variations: Greet children and elders the same way.
Keep it for one person you find difficult.
Bow your head a little as you say it.

practices.name: A raga for the hour
practices.instructions: Hindustani classical music assigns ragas to times of day. Play a raga meant for the afternoon, such as Bhimpalasi or Multani, and listen for fifteen minutes with your eyes closed. Do not look for a tune to hum. Follow how the player slowly opens the mode, note by note. Compare the mood to the light in your window.
practices.why: Raga is the melodic framework of Indian classical music, and each has a mood and an hour. Listening in the right hour makes the music feel like part of the day.
variations: Play a morning raga at dawn tomorrow.
Listen to a sitar, then a flute, then a voice.
Sit with a cup of tea while it plays.

practices.name: Tell a story from the epics
practices.instructions: Tell a short story from the Ramayana, the Mahabharata or the Panchatantra to a child or friend, or retell it to yourself in a notebook. Choose a small one, such as Hanuman’s leap, Savitri and Satyavan or the monkey and the crocodile. Tell it with voices and pauses, as storytellers do. End with one line about what it teaches.
practices.why: The epics and fables have been told aloud for thousands of years, to children and gatherings. Telling one yourself brings it to life.
variations: Tell it in two minutes, then in five.
Draw one scene from it.
Let the listener ask a question at the end.

practices.name: The evening lamp
practices.instructions: At dusk light a small lamp or candle. Stand before it with your palms together. If you like, circle your hand slowly in front of the flame three times as families do in aarti. Then sit and go through the day: where did you do well, where did you fall short, who needs your kindness tomorrow. Blow out the flame gently when you are done, with a thank you.
practices.why: Lighting a lamp at dusk is a daily household act in Hindu homes. The flame marks the shift from work to rest and gives the day a quiet closing.
variations: Use a clay lamp with a cotton wick and oil.
Place the lamp at the window to welcome the evening.
Light it before the family meal.

practices.name: The guest comes first
practices.instructions: Before you eat, serve someone else: a family member, a visitor, a neighbour, or put aside a portion for someone who is not there. Offer the best of it. Then eat quietly, without screens, with gratitude. Atithi devo bhava, the guest is like a god, is a rule of the Hindu home. Feed someone before you eat.
practices.why: Hospitality is a duty in Hindu households, where food offered to a guest is considered a blessing. Serving first is a simple, joyful habit.
variations: Cook a little more than you need and share it.
Wash up for the cook.
Eat the first bite slowly and silently.

practices.name: Sing a bhajan
practices.instructions: Choose a simple devotional song, a bhajan, and sing it quietly with a recording: Raghupati Raghava Raja Ram, Hare Krishna, or a song of Mirabai. You do not have to believe anything. Singing together is a warm way to end the day. Sit comfortably, tap the rhythm, and let the repetition carry you. Sing it again if you like.
practices.why: Bhajans are simple songs of devotion sung in homes and temples, easy to join even for a first-timer. Repeating a melody calms the mind.
variations: Sing with a family member or friend.
Hum the tune without words.
Learn the chorus of one bhajan this week.

practices.name: Did I harm anyone?
practices.instructions: Sit quietly and look back over the day with one question: did I harm any living thing today, in word, thought or deed? If so, how can I make it right? Note it in a line and make a plan to fix it tomorrow. Then recall one moment when you helped, and be glad. Ahimsa is not only about big violence but about small unkindnesses.
practices.why: Ahimsa, non-harm, is the first principle of Hindu and Jain ethics and a guide for the whole day. A short review at night keeps it alive.
variations: Write the day’s harms and helps in two columns.
Forgive one person for one thing.
Say sorry to someone you wronged.

practices.name: A story from the epics before sleep
practices.instructions: Read a few pages from the Ramayana or the Mahabharata, or from a children’s version, before sleep. R. K. Narayan’s retelling is short and lively. Read slowly and aloud if someone is with you. Stop at a good place. The epics were told in the evening by the fire, and they still make a gentle bedtime.
practices.why: The Ramayana and Mahabharata are the great stories of Hindu life, told for centuries at the end of the day. A short reading is a relaxing ritual.
variations: Read a children’s illustrated version.
Read just one chapter a night.
Listen to a recorded reading with the lights off.

practices.name: A dusk gaze
practices.instructions: In the hour of twilight go to a window, a roof or a doorway and watch the light change for ten minutes. Say nothing. Hindu households keep the hour of sandhya, the junction between day and night, as a time for stillness. Let the colours do the work. When the first lamp comes on, go in.
practices.why: Sandhya, the junctures of the day, are held to be times when the world is especially open. Pausing at dusk is one of the simplest ways to feel that.
variations: Look for the first star.
Sit outside with a cup of chai.
Close your eyes for the last minute.

practices.name: A kolam for a guest
practices.instructions: Make a large floor pattern at your entrance with rice flour, coloured chalk or flower petals, for a guest who is coming or in honour of a day. Plan it first on paper: a grid of dots, a border, a flower in the middle. Take your time, and enjoy the care. When people walk over it, let it go.
practices.why: Kolam and rangoli are welcome signs drawn at doorways in Indian homes. Making them slowly is meditative and sociable, and letting them go is the lesson.
variations: Make it with children.
Make it with petals gathered from the garden.
Make it on a pavement for passers-by.

practices.name: A night of small lamps
practices.instructions: Set out as many small lights as you have, tealights, candles or little oil lamps, along the windowsills, steps and tables. Turn off the electric lights. Make or buy one sweet, and give a plate to a neighbour. Sit for a while among the flames and let your eyes soften. This is the spirit of Diwali, the festival of lights, borrowed for one evening.
practices.why: Diwali is kept with rows of small lamps, sweets and visits to friends, and it celebrates the triumph of light over darkness. A modest version brings its warmth into any home.
variations: Light a lamp for a person you miss.
Make rangoli at the door first.
Take sweets to a neighbour.

immersePlan.name: Read a chapter of the Bhagavad Gita
immersePlan.text: Read one chapter of the Gita, the dialogue on a battlefield between Arjuna and Krishna. Pick out one line about action and its results, and copy it out.

immersePlan.name: Read a short Upanishad
immersePlan.text: Read a few pages of the Upanishads in Olivelle’s translation, such as the story of the student who learns to see the self in all things. Notice the questions.

immersePlan.name: Read a section of Narayan’s Ramayana
immersePlan.text: Read R. K. Narayan’s short retelling of the Ramayana and stop when a scene stirs you. Tell it in your own words to someone later.

immersePlan.name: Watch Pather Panchali
immersePlan.text: Watch Satyajit Ray’s 1955 film of a poor family in a Bengal village and the children’s wonder at a passing train. Notice the small joys.

immersePlan.name: Watch a part of Peter Brook’s Mahabharata
immersePlan.text: Watch a long stretch of Peter Brook’s 1989 staging of the great epic with a mixed cast. Notice how little is needed on the stage.

immersePlan.name: Watch Sita Sings the Blues
immersePlan.text: Watch Nina Paley’s animated retelling of the Ramayana, with Sita sung by a 1920s jazz voice, which she released free for anyone to share. Watch it with someone.

immersePlan.name: Listen to the Vishnu Sahasranamam
immersePlan.text: Play M. S. Subbulakshmi’s recitation of the thousand names. You do not need to follow the words. Let the sound of her voice fill the room for a while.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Call of the Valley
immersePlan.text: Play the 1967 classic of santoor, bamboo flute and guitar, made as a picture of a day in the Kashmir valley. Listen from morning to night in its movements.

immersePlan.name: Listen to the bhajans of Mirabai
immersePlan.text: Play the songs of the sixteenth-century poet-saint Mirabai, sung by Lata Mangeshkar and others. Notice the longing in the melodies.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Chola Nataraja
immersePlan.text: Look at the bronze of Shiva dancing in a ring of fire, one foot on a dwarf, the hair flying out. Trace the circle with your eye, and follow the hands.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Descent of the Ganges
immersePlan.text: Look at the vast rock relief at Mamallapuram with gods, animals and sages watching the river come down. Find the elephant family and the cat that is praying.

immersePlan.name: Look at Krishna and Radha in a Grove
immersePlan.text: Look at the small, tender Kangra painting of the two lovers among trees. Notice the colours, the flowers and the way the landscape holds them.

immersePlan.name: Cook a pot of khichdi
immersePlan.text: Simmer rice and split mung beans with a little turmeric and ghee until soft. It is the simple, comforting food of the Indian home. Serve it with yogurt.

immersePlan.name: Eat a vegetarian thali
immersePlan.text: Put dal, a vegetable, rice, a flatbread, yogurt and a pickle on a large plate. Eat with your right hand if you like, and taste each part before mixing.

immersePlan.name: Make or taste laddu
immersePlan.text: Roast chickpea flour in ghee, add sugar and cardamom and roll into balls. It is an offering sweet shared at festivals. Give one away before you eat one.

immersePlan.name: Boil a pot of masala chai
immersePlan.text: Boil black tea with milk, ginger and cardamom. The street sellers of India pull it high between two pots. Serve it to a friend and sit for a while.

immersePlan.name: Make a lassi
immersePlan.text: Beat yogurt with water and a little sugar or salt until frothy. Pour it over ice. Add cardamom or a spoon of mango pulp if you like.

immersePlan.name: Taste panchamrita
immersePlan.text: Mix milk, yogurt, honey, ghee and sugar in a small bowl, as is done for temple offerings. Take one spoonful and share the rest. Pay attention to the five flavours together.

immersePlan.name: Greet everyone with namaste
immersePlan.text: Greet each person you meet today with palms together at the heart and a slight bow. Say namaste if it feels natural. Notice how it feels to give and receive it.

immersePlan.name: Take your shoes off at the door
immersePlan.text: Leave your shoes at the door of your home today and have guests do the same. In India it is a mark of respect for the home and keeps the floor clean for sitting.

immersePlan.name: Draw a rangoli
immersePlan.text: Draw a rangoli or kolam at your threshold with chalk or flour. Begin with a grid of dots and join them with curves. Let it be wiped away.

immersePlan.name: Play pachisi
immersePlan.text: Play the cross-shaped race game that Akbar is said to have played in a courtyard with living pieces. Use a ludo set or draw the board. Roll cowries or dice.

immersePlan.name: Play Moksha Patam
immersePlan.text: Play snakes and ladders, which began in India as a lesson that virtue lifts you and vice drags you down. Play a game and name a virtue at each ladder.

immersePlan.name: Play Raji: An Ancient Epic
immersePlan.text: Play an hour of the action game set in ancient India, with painted scenery and a girl who fights demons with the help of the gods. Notice the art.

immersePlan.name: Mark Diwali
immersePlan.text: Diwali is a five-day festival of lights in autumn. Light a lamp this evening, make a sweet and share it with a neighbour or friend. Say happy Diwali.

immersePlan.name: Look up Holi
immersePlan.text: Holi, the spring festival of colour at the full moon in March, is kept with coloured powder, songs and sweets. Look at pictures, and learn why it is played. Use natural colours and protect eyes.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Meenakshi Temple
immersePlan.text: Look at the towers of Madurai’s temple, covered with thousands of coloured figures. Pick a tower and find five different figures.

immersePlan.name: Practise ahimsa
immersePlan.text: Ahimsa is non-harm. Today, avoid causing harm in a small way you normally ignore: crushing an insect, a cutting remark, wasting food.

immersePlan.name: Practise darshan
immersePlan.text: Darshan is seeing and being seen by the sacred. Look at one thing today with your whole attention for a full minute, as if it were looking back.

immersePlan.name: Share prasad
immersePlan.text: Prasad is food that has been offered and then shared. Cook or buy something small, offer it first to someone else, and enjoy what is left.

rules.text: Begin the day clean and with an offering
rules.why: Wash, then give something before you take anything: water, a flower, a moment of thanks.

rules.text: Do the work and release the result
rules.why: Give each task your full care. Leave praise, blame and reward to arrive when they will.
Eat no meat, speak no cruelty and step around the insect. Ahimsa covers act, word and thought.
A guest, a neighbour, a bird, a plant. No meal is only for yourself.
Contact one of them today: a call, a letter, a visit, a word of thanks.
A page of scripture, a hymn, a good friend. Give at least ten minutes to something that lifts the mind.

read.title: The Bhagavad Gita
read.creator: trans. Laurie L. Patton, or Barbara Stoler Miller
read.year: about 2nd century BCE to 2nd century CE
read.why: Seven hundred verses on a battlefield: a warrior who cannot act and a god who teaches him how to. The best door into the tradition.

read.title: The Upanishads
read.creator: trans. Patrick Olivelle
read.why: The dialogues in which teachers and students search for the self. Read the Katha and the Chandogya first.

read.title: The Ramayana
read.creator: retold by R. K. Narayan
read.why: The story of Rama, Sita and Hanuman in two hundred light pages by a great Indian novelist.

read.title: The Mahabharata: A Modern Rendering
read.creator: Ramesh Menon
read.why: The vast epic of a family war in which nobody is simply right. A readable prose version.

read.title: Speaking of Siva
read.creator: trans. A. K. Ramanujan
read.why: Short, fierce devotional poems by the Kannada saints of the twelfth century, who had no patience for ritual without love.

read.title: Darsan: Seeing the Divine Image in India
read.creator: Diana L. Eck
read.why: A short classic on why Hindus go to look at God, and what an image is.

watch.title: Pather Panchali
watch.creator: Satyajit Ray
watch.why: Village life in Bengal through a child’s eyes. Ritual, poverty and beauty with no explanation added.

watch.title: The Mahabharata
watch.creator: Peter Brook
watch.why: A long, spare staging of the epic with an international cast. Uneven, serious and unforgettable in places.

watch.title: Sita Sings the Blues
watch.creator: Nina Paley
watch.why: The Ramayana told from Sita’s side with shadow puppets and 1920s jazz. Three narrators argue about the details, as families do.

watch.title: Short Cut to Nirvana: Kumbh Mela
watch.creator: Maurizio Benazzo and Nick Day
watch.why: A documentary walk through the largest religious gathering on earth.

listen.title: Vishnu Sahasranamam
listen.creator: M. S. Subbulakshmi
listen.why: The thousand names of Vishnu sung by the most loved voice in South Indian music. Played in countless homes at dawn.

listen.title: Call of the Valley
listen.creator: Shivkumar Sharma, Hariprasad Chaurasia and Brij Bhushan Kabra
listen.why: A day in Kashmir told in ragas, from morning to night. A gentle first record of Indian classical music.

listen.title: Hanuman Chalisa
listen.creator: Many singers; try the version by Hariharan
listen.why: Forty verses in praise of Hanuman by the poet Tulsidas. Many people know all of it by heart.

listen.title: Bhajans of Mirabai
listen.creator: Sung by Lata Mangeshkar and others
listen.why: Love songs to Krishna by a Rajput princess who walked away from her palace.

art.title: Shiva as Lord of the Dance (Nataraja)
art.creator: Chola bronze casters, Tamil Nadu
art.why: Shiva dances the world into being and out again inside a ring of fire, one foot on ignorance. Fine examples are in Chennai, New York and Amsterdam.

art.title: Kandariya Mahadeva Temple
art.creator: Khajuraho, Madhya Pradesh
art.why: A stone mountain of towers rising to a peak, its walls crowded with gods, dancers and lovers.

art.title: Descent of the Ganges
art.creator: Mamallapuram, Tamil Nadu
art.why: A cliff face carved with gods, sages and a family of elephants, all turned toward the river coming down from heaven.

art.title: Krishna and Radha in a Grove
art.creator: Kangra school of painting
art.why: Small paintings from the Himalayan foothills in which the love of Radha and Krishna stands for the soul and God.

eat.title: Khichdi
eat.creator: Rice and split mung beans cooked soft with turmeric and ghee
eat.why: The plainest and most trusted meal in India. Offered in temples and given to the sick.

eat.title: A vegetarian thali
eat.creator: Dal, vegetables, rice, bread, yogurt and pickle on one plate
eat.why: A whole meal that balances the six tastes. Eaten with the right hand.

eat.title: Laddu
eat.creator: Chickpea flour, ghee and sugar rolled into balls
eat.why: The favourite sweet of Ganesha and the usual prasad at his festival.

eat.title: Curd rice
eat.creator: Rice mixed with yogurt, tempered with mustard seeds and curry leaves
eat.why: The cooling last course of a South Indian meal and a standard temple offering.

drink.title: Masala chai
drink.creator: Black tea boiled with milk, sugar, ginger and cardamom
drink.why: Not ancient, since tea drinking spread in India in the twentieth century, but now part of every day and every welcome.

drink.title: Lassi
drink.creator: Yogurt beaten with water, sweet or salted
drink.why: Cooling and old. Thinner versions are called chaas or buttermilk.

drink.title: Panchamrita
drink.creator: Milk, yogurt, ghee, honey and sugar
drink.why: The five nectars used to bathe a deity and then shared a spoonful at a time.

customs.title: Namaste
customs.creator: Palms together at the heart
customs.why: The greeting and the gesture of worship are the same. Bow the head slightly to elders.

customs.title: Shoes off
customs.creator: At the door of a home or temple
customs.why: Leather and street dust stay outside. Feet are not pointed at people, books or images.

customs.title: Touching the feet of elders
customs.creator: A bow and a blessing
customs.why: Younger people bend to touch an elder’s feet and receive a hand on the head. Only do this where it is clearly welcome.

customs.title: Rangoli and kolam
customs.creator: Patterns at the threshold
customs.why: Designs drawn in rice flour or coloured powder each morning to welcome guests and good fortune. Ants eat the flour, which is part of the point.

games.title: Pachisi
games.creator: Board game · India
games.why: A cross-shaped race game played with cowrie shells. The emperor Akbar is said to have played it on a courtyard with people as pieces. Ludo descends from it.

games.title: Snakes and Ladders (Moksha Patam)
games.creator: Board game · India
games.why: Made as a lesson in karma: ladders stand for virtues, snakes for vices and the last square for release.

games.title: Raji: An Ancient Epic
games.creator: Video game · Nodding Heads Games
games.why: A girl chosen by Durga fights demons to save her brother, through levels drawn from temple and shadow-puppet art. Made in Pune.

festivals.title: Diwali
festivals.creator: October or November, five days
festivals.why: The festival of lights. Lamps are set in every window for the return of Rama and the welcome of Lakshmi. Sweets, new clothes and fireworks.

festivals.title: Holi
festivals.creator: March, at the full moon
festivals.why: The spring festival of colour. A bonfire the night before, then a morning when everyone throws powder at everyone.

festivals.title: Navaratri and Durga Puja
festivals.creator: September or October, nine nights
festivals.why: Nine nights for the Goddess. Circle dances in Gujarat, great clay images of Durga in Bengal.

festivals.title: Maha Shivaratri
festivals.creator: February or March
festivals.why: The great night of Shiva, kept with fasting and a vigil until dawn.

festivals.title: Kumbh Mela
festivals.creator: Every three years, in turn at four river cities
festivals.why: Tens of millions gather to bathe at an auspicious hour. The largest is at Prayagraj every twelve years.

places.title: Varanasi
places.creator: Uttar Pradesh, India
places.why: The city of Shiva on the Ganges. Go to the river steps before dawn and again for the evening lamp ceremony. Cremations are private rites, so do not photograph them.

places.title: Meenakshi Temple
places.creator: Madurai, Tamil Nadu, India
places.why: A temple city inside a city, with towers covered in thousands of painted figures. Some inner shrines are open to Hindus only.

places.title: Rishikesh and Haridwar
places.creator: Uttarakhand, India
places.why: Where the Ganges leaves the Himalayas. Ashrams, pilgrims and the evening aarti at Har Ki Pauri.

places.title: Hampi
places.creator: Karnataka, India
places.why: The ruined capital of the Vijayanagara empire among boulders, with one great temple still in worship.

places.title: Uluwatu and Besakih
places.creator: Bali, Indonesia
places.why: Balinese Hinduism has its own calendar, offerings and temples. Dress as asked and stay out of the inner courts during ceremonies.

ethics.title: Dharma comes first
ethics.text: Each person has duties that come with their place: as child, parent, worker, neighbour, citizen. Doing your own duty imperfectly is held to be better than doing another’s well.
ethics.practice: Write down the three roles that make the strongest claim on you. Do one thing for the one you have neglected.

ethics.title: Ahimsa
ethics.text: Non-harming is called the highest duty. It asks for restraint in what you eat, how you speak and what you wish on others.
ethics.practice: Go through today without one harsh word, including about people who are not present.

ethics.title: Truthfulness
ethics.text: Satya means matching your words to what is so, and saying it in a way that does not injure. An old verse advises: say what is true and say what is pleasant.
ethics.practice: Before you speak today, check each thing against two tests: is it true and is it kind.

ethics.title: Giving
ethics.text: Dana is giving without contempt, to the right person at the right time, and expecting nothing back. The Gita calls any other gift tainted.
ethics.practice: Give something today that you will miss a little.

ethics.title: The guest is God
ethics.text: The Taittiriya Upanishad tells the student to treat mother, father, teacher and guest as divine. Hospitality is a religious act.
ethics.practice: Offer food or drink to the next person who comes to your door.

ethics.title: Self-restraint
ethics.text: Dama, mastery of the senses, is what makes every other virtue possible. A person pulled about by appetite cannot keep a promise.
ethics.practice: Choose one craving today and let it pass once without feeding it.

philosophy.title: The four aims of life
philosophy.text: A full life has four goals: dharma, living rightly; artha, earning well; kama, enjoying love and beauty; and moksha, freedom. None is despised. Trouble comes when one crowds out the rest.
philosophy.practice: Divide yesterday’s waking hours among the four aims. Which had none?

philosophy.title: Karma
philosophy.text: Actions shape the one who does them. A generous act makes a generous person and a cruel one hardens. The law is closer to cause and effect than to reward and punishment.
philosophy.practice: Trace one difficulty in your life back to a habit of your own. Start the opposite habit today, once.

philosophy.title: Three paths
philosophy.text: The Gita describes three ways to freedom: selfless action, knowledge and devotion. People differ, and the tradition expects them to climb by different roads.
philosophy.practice: Decide which of the three is most natural to you. Take one step on the one that is least natural.

philosophy.title: Many forms, one reality
philosophy.text: Hindus worship Vishnu, Shiva, the Goddess, Ganesha and thousands of local deities. Most understand them as faces of a single reality that is too large for one name.
philosophy.practice: Notice something sacred in three different places today: a person, an animal and a place.

philosophy.title: The self is not the body
philosophy.text: As a person takes off worn clothes and puts on new ones, says the Gita, so the self takes on new bodies. What you are does not age.
philosophy.practice: Sit for five minutes and watch your thoughts as you would watch traffic. Ask who is watching.

philosophy.title: The four stages
philosophy.text: Life has seasons: learning, building a household, stepping back and letting go. Each has its duties, and what is right at twenty-five may be wrong at seventy.
philosophy.practice: Name your stage. Name one thing you are doing that belongs to an earlier one.

philosophy.title: Lila
philosophy.text: The world is described as God’s play: made from fullness, for delight. Seen this way, life is something to take part in wholeheartedly without gripping it.
philosophy.practice: Do one thing today purely for the joy of it, with no purpose and no record.

philosophy.title: Seeing the same self in all
philosophy.text: The wise person, says the Gita, sees the same in a learned priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog and an outcaste. Every hierarchy is answered by this line.
philosophy.practice: Greet the person you would normally overlook with full attention.

intro: Hinduism is the name outsiders gave to the religious life of the Indian subcontinent. It has no founder, no single scripture and no central authority. Many Hindus prefer to call it sanatana dharma, the eternal way. It is practised today by about 1.2 billion people, and it is better understood as a family of traditions that share a vocabulary than as one system.

What they share is roughly this. There is an order to the world, called dharma, and each person has a part in keeping it. Actions have consequences that follow the doer, called karma. The self passes through many lives, and the final aim is freedom from that round, called moksha. There is one ultimate reality, and it can be approached through many forms: Vishnu and his descents as Rama and Krishna, Shiva, the Goddess in her many aspects, Ganesha who removes obstacles, and countless others.

The oldest texts are the four Vedas, hymns and ritual instructions composed in Sanskrit more than three thousand years ago and passed on by memory. The Upanishads, added at their end, turn from ritual to the search for the self. Most people, however, have learned their religion from the two great epics, the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, and from the Puranas, the story collections of the gods. The Bhagavad Gita, a short dialogue inside the Mahabharata, is the most widely read Hindu book.

Daily religion is concrete. It is a lamp lit at a household shrine, a mark on the forehead, a fast on a certain weekday, a visit to a temple to see the deity and be seen, food offered and shared, a pilgrimage to a river. It is also music, dance, sculpture and festivals that fill the streets. Philosophy runs alongside all of this, from strict non-dualism to warm devotional theism. The Vedanta Onda in this app follows one of those philosophical schools in depth.

This Onda follows the householder’s path, which is the path of most Hindus: begin the day clean and with an offering, do your work as service without clinging to its result, repeat a holy name, serve someone, and light a lamp at dusk. You are a guest here. Nothing asks you to worship any deity or to take on rites that belong to initiation or to a family line.

Two cautions. Hindu society has been shaped for centuries by caste, a hierarchy of birth that many Hindus, from the medieval poet-saints to B. R. Ambedkar and countless people today, have fought as a betrayal of the teaching that the same self lives in all. And Hindu symbols and words, from Om to karma to yoga, are often borrowed carelessly. The practice is to learn what they mean to the people who live by them.
guide.origin: The Indian subcontinent, and today Nepal, Bali, Mauritius, the Caribbean and a worldwide diaspora
guide.era: The oldest hymns date from about 1500 BCE. The tradition has never stopped changing since

figures.name: Yajnavalkya
figures.bio: The great sage of the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, who teaches the self by saying what it is not. His debates with Gargi and his wife Maitreyi are among the oldest philosophy in the world.

figures.name: Valmiki
figures.bio: The poet credited with the Sanskrit Ramayana. Legend makes him a robber who was changed by repeating a holy name.

figures.name: Adi Shankara
figures.bio: The philosopher who argued that the self and ultimate reality are one, and who is credited with founding monasteries at the four corners of India.

figures.name: Andal
figures.bio: A Tamil poet-saint, the only woman among the twelve Alvars. Her thirty-verse Tiruppavai is still sung every winter dawn.

figures.name: Ramanuja
figures.bio: The theologian of devotion, who held that souls are real, distinct and held within a personal God. He opened temple worship to lower castes.

figures.name: Basava
figures.bio: A minister in Karnataka who led a movement of Shiva devotees rejecting caste and temple ritual. Its short poems, the vachanas, are still loved.

figures.name: Mirabai
figures.bio: A Rajput princess who took Krishna as her only husband, left court life and wandered singing. Her songs are known across North India.

figures.name: Tulsidas
figures.bio: The poet who retold the Ramayana in the everyday language of North India. His Ramcharitmanas is recited and staged every autumn.

figures.name: Swami Vivekananda
figures.bio: A monk from Calcutta whose speech at the Parliament of Religions in Chicago in 1893 introduced Hindu thought to a wide Western public.

figures.name: Mohandas K. Gandhi
figures.bio: He read the Gita daily as a manual of selfless action and made non-violence and truth the tools of a political struggle.

history.detail: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa had baths, seals and figurines that some scholars link to later practice. Their script is unread, so the links remain uncertain.
More than a thousand hymns to Agni, Indra and other powers, composed in early Sanskrit and handed down by exact oral recitation, which continues today.
Forest teachers turn inward and ask what the self is. The ideas of karma, rebirth and release take shape. The Buddha and Mahavira teach in the same period.
The Mahabharata and the Ramayana grow over centuries into their present size. The Bhagavad Gita is composed within the first.
The first stone temples, classical Sanskrit poetry and the Puranas. Worship of images in temples becomes the main form of public religion.
The Alvars and Nayanars sing to Vishnu and Shiva in Tamil, in the people’s language. The devotional movement they begin spreads north over the next thousand years.
Shankara’s commentaries make Advaita Vedanta the most influential Hindu philosophy among scholars.
Thanjavur, Khajuraho, Konark and Angkor Wat in Cambodia, which was built for Vishnu. Hindu kingdoms flourish across Southeast Asia.
Kabir, Mirabai, Surdas, Chaitanya and Tulsidas preach and sing a religion of love that questions caste and empty ritual, much of it under Muslim rule.
Ram Mohan Roy, Dayananda Saraswati and others campaign against widow burning and child marriage and argue over what the tradition really teaches.
His address to the Parliament of the World’s Religions, opening with a greeting to his sisters and brothers of America, begins the modern global presence of Hinduism.
India becomes independent and is partitioned. The constitution, drafted under B. R. Ambedkar, outlaws untouchability.
Migration carries temples to every continent. Yoga and meditation become global, and debates about identity, caste and politics continue within India.

concepts.text: The order of things and one’s part in it.
concepts.detail: From a root meaning to hold. It covers law, duty, virtue and religion. Texts distinguish the duties common to everyone, such as truth and non-harming, from those that belong to a role or a stage of life.

The self carries the traces of what it has done into new births. The idea explains difference without blaming a god, and it puts responsibility on the doer. It has also been misused to justify inequality.
Freedom from the round of birth and death. Schools differ on what it is: the self knowing itself as ultimate reality, or the soul living forever in the presence of God.

concepts.text: The ground of all and the self.
concepts.detail: The Upanishads teach that the reality behind the world and the reality behind the person are the same. The schools of Vedanta disagree about how exactly.
Brahma creates, Vishnu preserves and Shiva dissolves. In practice most Hindus are devoted to Vishnu, to Shiva or to the Goddess, Shakti, as the supreme.
Vishnu is said to descend whenever dharma declines. Ten descents are usually listed, including the fish, the boar, Rama, Krishna and, in many lists, the Buddha.
The deity present in an image is woken, bathed, dressed, fed and put to rest. The worshipper comes to see and be seen, and takes home food that has been blessed.
Devotion to a personal God, open to everyone whatever their birth, sex or learning. It produced most of the poetry and music of the tradition.
Karma yoga, jnana yoga and bhakti yoga are set out in the Bhagavad Gita as routes suited to different temperaments. Later teachers added the discipline of meditation as a fourth.

concepts.text: What was heard and what is remembered.
concepts.detail: The Vedas and Upanishads are held to be revealed. Epics, law books and Puranas are remembered tradition, with less authority and far more readers.

facts.text: The number 108 turns up everywhere: beads on a mala, names of a deity, sun salutations. Explanations vary and none is official.
The Mahabharata has about one hundred thousand verses, roughly seven times the Iliad and the Odyssey together.
Angkor Wat in Cambodia, the largest religious monument in the world, was built in the twelfth century as a temple to Vishnu.
Vedic recitation is passed on with such exact methods of cross-checking that UNESCO listed it as intangible heritage in 2008.
The swastika is an ancient sign of good fortune in Hindu, Jain and Buddhist use. Its meaning there has nothing to do with its abuse in twentieth century Europe.
Bali is a Hindu-majority island in a Muslim-majority country, with a tradition that developed on its own for a thousand years.

sensitivity.note: Hinduism is a living religion of more than a billion people and enormous variety. This Onda offers a guest’s version of the householder’s day. It does not ask you to worship any deity, and it leaves out rites that need initiation, a priest or a family tradition.
requiredCaveats: No single account fits all Hindus. Practice differs by region, language, community and family.
Sacred images, words and symbols such as Om are objects of worship. Treat them with the care their owners do.
Caste has caused great suffering and is opposed by many Hindus. Nothing here endorses it.
In temples, follow local rules on dress, shoes, photography and which areas are open to visitors.
